summary:
A Moon base will likely run at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, air that makes materials much more flammable than on Earth. Has NASA ever tested fire in that air? The answer is in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, but it is spread across 19 flight investigations, each with its own tables and units.

Ember Atlas puts it on one map. We cleaned NASA's tables into 2,940 tests, each traceable to its original cell, and plotted the 1,022 that record both room oxygen and pressure. Pick a habitat (the ISS, a Moon base or rover, Earth air or an oxygen-rich hospital ward) and Ember Atlas shows, for each fire-safety job (prevent, detect, suppress) and fuel (gas, liquid, solid), whether NASA has tested it there. It opens the NASA row behind every number and proposes the next tests to close each gap.

The finding: only 20 tests ran in Moon-base air, all of them gas flames. Solid materials never went above 22.2% oxygen in NASA's tables, and no smoke-detection test records the air it ran in. Those are the tests a Moon base still needs.
details:
THE QUESTION

A Moon base will likely run at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, between a spacesuit and Earth's air, and the challenge notes that this makes materials much more flammable. Ember Atlas answers one question for anyone designing such a habitat: has NASA tested fire in this air, for each part of fire safety?

WHAT IT DOES

1. Pick a habitat: the ISS cabin, a Moon base or pressurized rover, Earth air, or an oxygen-rich hospital ward. The API also accepts any custom zone, such as a planned Mars habitat.

2. Read the verdict: a grid of NASA's three fire-safety jobs (prevent, detect, suppress) by fuel (gas, liquid, solid). Each cell is TESTED (3 or more tests inside the zone), NEAR (at least one test within a stated distance), NOT RECORDED (tests exist, but NASA's table leaves out their oxygen or pressure), PLANNED or UNTESTED.

3. Open the proof: any number opens the NASA table line it came from, re-read from NASA's file with its SHA-256 checked, together with the investigation's DOI and every cleaning step applied.

4. Get the next tests: a designer proposes 3 to 12 test points that cover the zone evenly, optionally limited to breathable air (oxygen partial pressure of 2.6 to 3.1 psia, from a NASA paper).

Also: an Atlas of every test, Compare for two habitats, an Earth mode, a Model page, Ask, and a Methods page with every source, rule and limit.

WHAT WE FOUND (computed from NASA's rows)

- Only 20 tests ran in Moon-base air. All are gas flames from one investigation (ACME CFI-G), at one pressure (7.35 psi).

- Solid materials such as fabrics and plastics never went above 22.2% oxygen in NASA's tables, and none of the 388 solid tests records its pressure.

- No detection-related test (SAME, SAME-R, DAFT, SPICE) records the oxygen or pressure it ran in, so detection cannot be checked for any habitat.

- Droplet flames came close: 17 FLEX tests at 30% oxygen or more ran at 10.33 to 10.5 psi, just above the Moon-base limit. FLEX-2's test plan (planned, not flown) reaches the zone for 8 fuels.

- Moon base: 1 of 9 cells TESTED, 2 NEAR, 6 NOT RECORDED. The ISS, Earth air and an oxygen-rich ward each have 3 TESTED cells and the same 6 gaps: solids and detection.

HOW IT MEETS THE CHALLENGE'S OBJECTIVES

- Identify relevant investigations: the verdict names the investigations and tests behind every cell, nearest first, for each habitat.

- Extract data for predictive modeling: one clean table of 2,940 tests (oxygen in %, pressure in psi, raw text and source line kept), exportable as CSV or JSON, plus two FLEX droplet models built on it that refuse inputs outside NASA's tested range.

- Highlight research for next-generation fire safety: the gaps in solids and detection, and the proposed test points, show where new tests and equipment work would matter most.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data: 24 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database: 19 flight investigations and 5 ground studies that re-analysed flight data. NASA's files are kept untouched, each with a SHA-256 checksum.

- Cleaning: one cleaner per investigation turns NASA's tables into 2,940 tests in 2,024 rows. Oxygen is always in % and pressure always in psi, with NASA's raw text kept beside every converted value, and every quirk follows a written rule (mislabelled columns, shorthand rows, blank padding rows, a test plan that is not tests). A data contract re-reads every cited cell and checks each investigation's row count; if any check fails, nothing is published.

- Live source check: a script compares our copy with NASA PSI's public web service. Last run (14 Nov 2026): 24 of 24 investigations present, 22 of 22 tables identical in size.

- Models: ridge regression for the FLEX burning-rate constant (R² 0.70 on unseen test dates, against 0.03 for a baseline; 0.28 when later campaigns are predicted from earlier ones) and logistic regression for self-extinction (balanced accuracy 0.67, ROC-AUC 0.83). Inputs outside the tested range are refused (HTTP 422). FLEX never burned below 10.18 psi, so the models refuse every Moon-base pressure instead of guessing.

- Where SI fits: Claude drafted the answers to five core questions, and our checker rejects any number that does not appear in a cited NASA source; these answers are labelled AI TEXT. We chose not to run an AI model live, so no unchecked number reaches a user. Any other question searches 18,487 passages from NASA's investigation records and 273 NASA technical papers.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Mission planners and fire-safety engineers see which habitat atmospheres have flight evidence, and which do not, without searching 19 investigations by hand.

- Researchers get a reproducible list of test points that would close the Moon-base gap.

- Data curators see where NASA's tables leave out oxygen or pressure, which is what makes solids and detection uncheckable today.

- On Earth, the same check covers oxygen-enriched rooms such as hospital wards, with a warning that microgravity results are not Earth predictions.

- Built to grow: when partial-gravity data such as LUCI and FM2 reach PSI, as the challenge expects, a new cleaner can put them on the same map.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It treats NASA's archive as evidence to audit, not just data to plot: every value carries a stamp (NASA, CONVERTED, DERIVED, MODEL, AI TEXT, PROPOSAL) and opens its source line.

- One map of NASA's fire tests by room oxygen and pressure, with the Moon base, the ISS and Earth drawn as zones.

- An honest safety answer: the verdict reports test coverage and refuses to predict where there is no data.

- Code-drawn flame renders (labelled RENDER) show why fire behaves differently when nothing lifts the hot gas.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python 3.11 with pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, FastAPI, Pydantic and Uvicorn; TypeScript with React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query and React Router; hand-built SVG charts and WebGL renders; no database. Tests: 354 pytest tests, 83 Vitest tests and 32 Playwright end-to-end checks with axe accessibility scans, plus ruff. No special hardware.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Never invent a value: if NASA's table does not state it, we store null and show NOT RECORDED.

- Units: oxygen is always in % and pressure always in psi, with NASA's raw text kept beside every converted value.

- No partial-gravity predictions: PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data, so we show coverage, not forecasts.

- Accessibility: keyboard use throughout, WCAG 2.1 AA checked by axe on every view at desktop and phone sizes, reduced motion respected.

- Resilience: if the backend sleeps, a static copy keeps the map, the preset verdicts and the evidence working.

- Credit: NASA PSI data is CC0-1.0, and every investigation is cited by its DOI. Ember Atlas is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

USE OF AI (SI)

We used Claude (Anthropic) through claude.ai and Claude Code. It drafted our planning documents, helped gather NASA's PSI files (checked against NASA's own file sizes), wrote most of the code under our review, drafted the five machine-checked answers (labelled AI TEXT on the site), and drafted the demo deck and this description. No AI runs on the site, and every number shown is computed from NASA's files by tested code. Our full AI-use log is docs/AI_USE.md in the repository.

LIMITS

- No verdict is a Moon or Mars prediction.

- Zone edges and the distance scale are design choices, each stated with its source.

- The Moon-base gas cell rests on one investigation at one pressure.

- FLEX's table mixes space and ground tests, so those rows are marked gravity unknown.
